source.title: Bag of Tricks for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts: A Benchmark Across Reasoning, Efficiency, and Safety
source.authors: Mu-Fan Qiu; Zhe-Yu Shen; Ping-Zhi Li; Ang Li; Tianlong Chen

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates MoE architecture and fine-tuning choices, but does not test or use the claimed scaling laws. It cites Kaplan et al. in background discussion.
record.gate_note: No held-out cross-entropy scaling sweep, small-to-large extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation test is reported. Figure 3 and its discussion report pretraining training-loss convergence across expert-granularity configurations; this is not a test of the claim's held-out scaling behavior. Other reasoning, efficiency, and safety results concern MoE design choices rather than the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is an MoE design benchmark covering reasoning accuracy, routing efficiency metrics and safety. It cites Kaplan et al. only as background. It reports no held-out loss sweep over parameters, data or compute, no extrapolation, and no compute-optimal fit. The expert-granularity training-loss curves are MoE routing choices measured as convergence speed. They are not V4's depth/width shape test at fixed parameter count with held-out loss, so they bear on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that MoE design choices trade off reasoning, efficiency and safety. They recommend full fine-tuning followed by router freezing (N→R) as a sweet-point strategy, and report that token-level routing and z-loss help reasoning while shared experts aid stability. They draw no scaling-law conclusions.
record.recipe_differences: The paper benchmarks MoE design choices rather than applying a scaling-law fitting or extrapolation method.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the scaling-law claim.

fits_no_version.finding: In small OLMoE-style MoE pretraining on Minipile, coarse-grained experts reach lower training loss faster than fine-grained experts. The gap is larger without auxiliary loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Expert granularity in MoE pretraining affects training-loss convergence speed, and auxiliary load-balancing loss moderates the effect.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code, checkpoints, and raw data will be released upon acceptance.
record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2025
record.problems: The convergence result is described qualitatively from plotted curves, without numeric loss values or reported uncertainty. The paper notes that experiments are limited to small-scale MoE models and cover only a subset of architectures and strategies.
record.rows_left_out: No other results are included: the remaining reported comparisons concern MoE reasoning accuracy, efficiency metrics, safety, or hallucination, not the scaling-law claim versions.

untested.parts: Not tested: no held-out loss as a function of parameters, tokens or compute.
Not tested: no fitted law extrapolated to larger runs.
Not tested: no depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count on held-out loss. The expert-granularity comparison is MoE-specific and reports only training-loss convergence.
Not tested: no power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
Not tested: no relation of downstream accuracy to scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: Accuracy differences across configurations are tiny (e.g. 65.35% vs 65.16% average), with no uncertainty reported. The Kaplan citation is background only.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute across several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as functions of compute.
Loss comparisons at fixed parameter count across depth, width, and other architectural variations.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: OLMoE
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-loss convergence across coarse- and fine-grained expert configurations.

conditions.value: Four expert-granularity settings; figure also distinguishes shared-expert, auxiliary-loss, and load-balancing settings

rows.value: Coarse-grained experts converge faster than fine-grained experts across all four settings.
rows.note: The paper states the direction of the convergence result, but does not give numeric loss values in the text. It compares pretraining training-loss curves, not held-out loss as a function of model size, data, or compute.
rows.check: The subject is questionable. The paper pretrains OLMoE-architecture variants on Minipile and says experiments are limited to small-scale MoE models. The '7 billion parameters' figure describes the released OLMoE model, not necessarily these pretraining runs. The measure is training-loss convergence speed across expert granularities, not held-out loss versus scale. The text is also internally inconsistent: one passage says fine-grained experts 'showed no clear advantage', another says coarse-grained experts converge faster.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
